questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/200dcd87827ae9683ba0ecb3b284509b31d32f9e0dc1b9736a260d2f7d71b0a0.png)

Rounded to **two decimal places**, the area of $△ABC$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}ac\operatorname{sin}⁡B,
$$

where $∠B$ is between the sides of lengths $a$ and $c.$ 

Here, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=5, \\ a & =BC=5, \\ m∠B & ={60}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘}=0.866\,025,
$$

rounded to six decimal places,  we calculate the area as follows:
 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5\cdot 5\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} \\  & =12.5\cdot (0.866\,025) \\  & ≈10.83,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to **two decimal places**.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/7ead42d83a971733b601f45dcc1ad545a52298fc8a800ba69344651a54f4830d.png)

The area of the acute triangle $△ABC$ is $20\sqrt{2}{\text{ cm}}^{2}.$ Then, the measure of $∠A$ is{{field-1}} ${}^{∘}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=8\,\text{cm}, \\ b & =AC=10\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate $m∠A$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 20\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 10\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 20\sqrt{2} & =40\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{20\sqrt{2}}{40} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡A & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ m∠A & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

The area of ​​the triangle $△ABC$ is $5\sqrt{3}\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.$ Find $AC.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=5\text{ cm}, \\ b & =AC, \\ m∠A & ={60}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $b=AC,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 5\sqrt{3} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 5\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{60}^{∘} \\ 5\sqrt{3} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 5\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ 5\sqrt{3} & =\frac{5\sqrt{3}\,b}{4} \\ \cancel{5\sqrt{3}} & =\frac{\cancel{5\sqrt{3}}\,b}{4} \\ 1 & =\frac{b}{4} \\ b & =4\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AC=4\,\text{cm}.$

The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=\sqrt{2}\,\text{ cm}, \\ b & =AC=\sqrt{6}\,\text{cm}\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2} & =\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \cancel{\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}} & =\cancel{\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 1 & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & =\operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡A & =\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \\ m∠A & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}

The area of ​​the triangle $△ABC$ is $\frac{25\sqrt{3}}{2}{\text{cm}}^{2}.$ Then,  $AC=${{field-1}} $\text{cm}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=10\text{ cm}, \\ b & =AC, \\ m∠A & ={120}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{120}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $b=AC,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{25\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 10\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{120}^{∘} \\ \frac{25\sqrt{3}}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot 10\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}) \\ \frac{25\sqrt{3}}{2} & =5b\cdot \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ 25\cancel{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} & =5b\cdot \cancel{\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}} \\ 5b & =25 \\ b & =5\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/dafaf2421aaa9be80c472b4dde7c941defb94f7f3533fda4ebb2fdcee2b60e31.png)

In square units rounded to the **nearest tenth**, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $△ABD$ and $△BDC$ (see the illustration below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/cd9363a3cc686ae45f49c982f4b31ad75b7c7897dcf7e8af58e530dba6946e1d.png)

First we find the area for $△ABD:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6\cdot 7\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘} \\  & =21\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{50}^{∘} \\  & ≈16.086\,9,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Now we find the area for $△BCD:$ 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{BDC} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 7\cdot 8\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘} \\  & =28\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{43}^{∘} \\  & ≈19.096\,0,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to four decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABD}+{A}_{BDC} \\  & ≈16.086\,9+19.096\,0 \\  & ≈35.182\,9\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the **nearest tenth**, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $35.2.$

questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/36af7324fd2112d94feddc5a1a02a91d97bbc0866cb93a6ca711dd73f566305a.png)

Find, to the nearest integer, the area of the parallelogram $ABCD.$
questions.worked_solution:
The diagonal $\overset{―}{AC}$ divides the parallelogram into two congruent triangles. Therefore, the area of the parallelogram is twice the area of $△ACB$ (see the illustration below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/7cfcb5cdf77b4afbf25afd64e37bb33f0ab2c211e09659181bfc16db0ccd2db7.png)

 Computing the area of $△ACB,$ we find
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ACD} & =\frac{1}{2}(18)(8)\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =72\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & ≈67.658,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places. Consequently,

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & =2{A}_{ACB} \\  & =2\cdot 67.658 \\  & =135.316.\end{aligned}
$$

So, to the nearest integer, the area of the parallelogram is $135.$

$$

Now we find the area for $△BCD:$

questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the area of $△ABD.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot AB\cdot AD\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 2.5\cdot 6\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{63}^{∘} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 15\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{63}^{∘} \\  & =6.682… \\  & ≈7{\text{ km}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the **nearest integer**.

The difference of the areas of $△ABD$ and the quadrilateral $ABCD$ gives the area of $△BCD.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△BCD} & ={A}_{△ABD}-{A}_{ABCD} \\  & =7-5 \\  & =2{\text{ km}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/d6923f5883ea770ce243eb23594740461a689c01f63de0421bc6f5d73a39531d.png)

The area of $ABCD$ is $7{\text{ mm}}^{2}.$   Then, the area of $△BCD$, rounded to the **nearest integer**, is{{field-1}}${\text{ mm}}^{2}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the area of $△ABD.$ We get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△ABD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot AB\cdot AD\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot 7\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 28\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\  & =9.899… \\  & ≈10{\text{ m}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the **nearest integer**.

The difference of the areas of $△ABD$ and the quadrilateral $ABCD$ gives the area of $△BCD.$ Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{△BCD} & ={A}_{△ABD}-{A}_{ABCD} \\  & =10-7 \\  & =3{\text{ mm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Area of a Triangle
canonical_examples.problem:
Find the area of $\triangle{ABC}$ below. Round your answer to two decimal places.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/dc625408598aa3cbfda44ec877c9a26ab563dee9fcf757192fcf2cf8411f606a.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
\mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}ab\sin{C},
$$

where $\angle{C}$ is between the sides of lengths $a$ and $b.$ 

Here, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}a & =CB=58 \\ b & =CA=40 \\ m∠C & ={31}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since 

$$
\sin{31^{\circ}} = 0.515\,038
$$

rounded to six decimal places,  we calculate the area as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 58\cdot 40\operatorname{sin}⁡{31}^{∘} \\  & =1160\cdot (0.515\,038) \\  & ≈597.44,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating an Angle or Side of a Triangle Given the Area of a Triangle
canonical_examples.problem:
The area of ​​the triangle $\triangle ABC$ is $24\sqrt{2} \text{ cm}^2.$ Find $AB.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/e93e732bd04cfda304c2098087548a638d8d869ccf8b1050235e8207825875d3.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
\mathcal{A}=\dfrac{1}{2}bc\sin{A},
$$

where $\angle{A}$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB, \\ b & =AC=12\text{ cm}, \\ m∠A & ={45}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\sin{45^{\circ}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $c=AB,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ 24\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{45}^{∘} \\ 24\sqrt{2} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 12\cdot c\cdot (\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}) \\ 24\cancel{\sqrt{2}} & =3\cancel{\sqrt{2}}c \\ 24 & =3c \\ c & =8\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AB = 8\,\textrm{cm}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Calculating the Area of a Quadrilateral
canonical_examples.problem:
Rounded to the nearest integer, what is the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/bc9f32a9c0e8b042498a72e808a29274bd505e786d8ec43d0e0bc9888fdf6e44.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is the sum of the areas of the triangles $\triangle ABC$ and $\triangle ADC$ (see the illustration below).

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/acd2e923a65d0821cd59ed8b8274ceb5fc38def896467e37c8b1d454f958699e.png)

 First, we find the area for $\triangle ABC,$ and get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABC} & =\frac{1}{2}(42)(35)\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘} \\  & =735\operatorname{sin}⁡{36}^{∘} \\  & ≈432.022\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Now we find the area for $\triangle ADC,$ and get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ADC} & =\frac{1}{2}(20)(18)\operatorname{sin}⁡{80}^{∘} \\  & =180\operatorname{sin}⁡{80}^{∘} \\  & ≈177.265\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to three decimal places.

Finally, we add together the areas of our two triangles to determine the area of $ABCD.$ We get
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABCD} & ={A}_{ABC}+{A}_{ADC} \\  & =432.022+177.265 \\  & ≈609\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, to the nearest integer, the area of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ is $609.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Area of a Triangle Given the Area of a Quadrilateral
canonical_examples.problem:
The area of $ABCD$ is $300\, \text{cm}^2.$  What is the area of $\triangle ABC$ rounded to the nearest integer?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13946476/assets/c06ffb123bdd24c3f83419767b6d1578223b8093089b79f91aae8f1fc6121305.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's start by finding the area of $\triangle ACD.$ We get 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ACD} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot DA\cdot DC\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡D \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(25)(32)\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =400\operatorname{sin}⁡{70}^{∘} \\  & =375.877... \\  & ≈376\,{\text{cm}}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest integer.

The difference of the areas of the quadrilateral $ABCD$ and $\triangle ACD$ gives the area of $\triangle ABC.$ Therefore, 
 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{ABC} & ={A}_{ACD}-{A}_{ABCD} \\  & =376-300 \\  & =76\,{\text{cm}}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
